description_full: Sonoco Products Company, together with its subsidiaries, designs, develops, manufactures, and sells various engineered and sustainable packaging products in the United States, Europe, Canada, the Asia Pacific, and internationally. The company operates in two segments, Consumer Packaging and Industrial Paper Packaging. The Consumer Packaging segment offers round and shaped rigid paper, steel, and plastic containers, as well as metal and peelable membrane ends, closures, and components. Its Industrial Paper Packaging segment provides paperboard tubes, cones, and cores; paper-based protective packaging; and uncoated recycled paperboards. The company also offers packaging materials, such as plastic, paper, foam, and various other specialty materials. It sells its products in various markets, including the paper, textile, film, food, packaging, construction, and wire and cable markets. The company was founded in 1899 and is headquartered in Hartsville, South Carolina.

CEO compensation is 10× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Sonoco Products Company is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $4.8B market cap on $7.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 10% against a 7% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 19% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $346M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.69×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.4×.

Shareholder yield of 4.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.8) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Very elevated short interest (15.1% of float) — sophisticated money is betting against the business
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 10% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Trading at a 56% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
Valued at a 29% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Consumer Cyclical sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

sect: Its 14% operating margin runs 6pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.70x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+6.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 21% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 16% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 19% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.77, it is more defensive than the market.
About $51.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 37% in the 2020 crash, 22% in the 2022 bear market and 51% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 56% below its DCF fair value of $112, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 57%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $73.39 to $171 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 8.5 vs 18.8 and EV/EBITDA 7.6 vs 10.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 49% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 7.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $57.12 on average, 17% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.23).
It runs a 19% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.69x.
ROE of 28% is amplified by 3.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.6x net debt to EBITDA ($378.4M of cash against $4.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.4x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.80 in the distress zone.
The Beneish M-score (-1.85) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.5% over 3 years, 6.9% over 5 years and 4.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 10.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -7.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (4.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 11, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.0%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 1 sale over the past year, net $234K bought.
It returns 4.5% a year to shareholders (0.2% in buybacks and 4.4% in dividends).
Short interest is elevated at 15.1% of the float, 9.0 days to cover.
people: With about 22,000 employees, each generates about $342K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 4.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $16K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.3M (10x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
